english.html: made himself revered by many with great wonder; persuading them, moreover, that all things were feasible by means of magical vanity <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>. And yet neither must one think that magic is altogether fabulous, seeing that the laws, both divine and human, have so often spoken of it, and commanded that it be exterminated from the earth as a thing abominable and full of impiety <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. These were certainly among the first ruses and principal wiles that this trickster and father of lies, Satan, set up to ruin and seduce men: even to having Simon the Samaritan adored as God, and a statue erected to him with this inscription, SIMONI DEO SANCTO, which is as much as to say, To Simon the holy God <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. Now this diabolical art (the invention of which is attributed to Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians, who wrote a hundred thousand verses <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>) is called Magic; although Magic of itself signifies nothing evil, but rather all sapience, wisdom and knowledge of things universally, both human and divine. But two kinds have been made of it: the one natural and permitted, the other ceremonial and reprobate. Natural Magic is an excellent learning and perfect knowledge of the secret virtues of nature, whether in celestial influences, stones or herbs; to learn which Pythagoras, Empedocles and Democritus voluntarily banished themselves from their native land, wandered as vagabonds through divers provinces, and travelled into far-off and foreign countries; and such Magic was of old in those noble and renowned wise men who came from the East to adore the little child Jesus Christ <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>; in Archytas of Tarentum also, who had made a dove of wood, balanced with counterweights, of such a structure and so ingenious a contrivance that it flew in the air of itself; moreover in Boethius, who made birds sing, and cows and bulls, made of metal, bellow <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>; and in Albert the Great, who made a head of brass speak; and other such. Ceremonial Magic is so called because it consists wholly in superstitions and ceremonies of words, names, images, characters, consecrations, sacrifices and other like vanities <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>, by which the

notes.citation: Pietro Crinito (Pierre Crinit), De honesta disciplina IX.5 (De magia Aegyptiorum … ac de daemonibus, et qua potestate polleant)
notes.original: Pierre Crinit au liure ix. de honeſta diſciplina. c. v
notes.gloss: Crinito, 1475–1507, the Florentine humanist; cited at annot-005 as well. On the devil's magic and its spread.

notes.citation: Deuteronomy 18 (18:10–12); Leviticus 20 (20:6, 27); Code 9.18 (De maleficis et mathematicis), l. 1 (C. 9.18.1) and the whole title; Decretum, C. 26 q. 5, the last canon (c. Nec mirum, c. 14; the print's xxxvj is a wrong sort for xxvj, since Causa 36 has no fifth question)
notes.original: Deutero. c. xviij. Leui. c. xx. l. j. & tout le titre. C. de malef. & mathemat. c. fin. xxxvj. q. v.
notes.gloss: The divine and human laws against magic: the sorcery title of the Code, which the case file §6.3 says to expect wherever Coras discusses magic, and Gratian's great canon on magical arts, from Augustine.

notes.citation: Tertullian, Apology (ch. 13: the Romans dedicated a statue to Simon Magus with the inscription Sancti Dei); Pietro Crinito, De honesta disciplina VIII.1 (De Simone Samarite, qui magus dicitur, from Tertullian's Apologeticum; the print's liu vij. is a slip for viij)
notes.original: Tertuliã en. ſon Apologetique. Pierre Crinit au liu vij. c. j.
notes.gloss: The inscription SIMONI DEO SANCTO is Justin Martyr's (First Apology 26) as well; it is a Christian reading of the Sabine god Semo Sancus's altar on the Tiber island.

notes.original: Pline au liure xxx. c. j.
notes.gloss: Pliny makes Zoroaster the inventor of magic and reports from Hermippus that he wrote two million lines (vicies centum milia versuum); Coras's "a hundred thousand" does not match. Pliny does not call him king of the Bactrians; that is the tradition of Justin and others.

notes.citation: Cassiodorus (Caſiodore), Variae (I.45, the letter to Boethius on the water-clock and sundial for Gundobad, which credits Boethius with Archytas's dove and with metal birds that sing and metal bulls that bellow); Pietro Crinito, De honesta disciplina XVII.12 in the Paris 1543 edition (De Archytae columba volatili … ac de Boethii philosophi pari ingenio, ex Cassiodori Variis; the print's c. xiij is one ahead)
notes.original: Caſiodore aux liures variarum Pierre Crinit au liure xvij. c. xiij.
notes.gloss: Cassiodorus is the source of Coras's whole list of natural-magic automata; the brazen head of Albert the Great is a later legend.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 26 q. 5, the last canon (c. Nec mirum, c. 14), at § Ad haec omnia
notes.original: c fin. P ad hæc omnia. xxvj. q. v.
notes.gloss: The same canon and paragraph cited at annot-022 {b}; its catalogue of the superstitious arts. The print's P is its sort for §.
